subject: biology
title: Action Potential Adventure
welcome_lead: Today you'll fire an action potential — depolarisation, repolarisation, hyperpolarisation, then refractory recovery.
meta_desc: A-Level Biology Nervous Coordination — action potential, +30 mV peak, refractory period, all-or-nothing principle.
final_note: You learned the four stages of the action potential, why it's all-or-nothing, and how the refractory period ensures one-way propagation.

concepts.def: ~ -55 mV — voltage at which Na+ channels open en masse
Na+ floods in → membrane potential rises to about +30 mV
Na+ channels close, K+ channels open → K+ rushes out, restoring negative inside
K+ channels slow to close → briefly more negative than -70 mV
Recovery time — no second AP possible until ions reset
Below threshold = nothing; at or above threshold = full AP every time

walkthroughs.body_html:
A stimulus opens some Na+ channels → small depolarisation.

If membrane reaches -55 mV (threshold), voltage-gated Na+ channels fly open.

Na+ rushes in down its gradient → rapid depolarisation to about +30 mV.

Inside the axon is briefly positive relative to outside — the spike of the action potential.

At the peak (+30 mV):
- Na+ channels close (inactivate)
- Voltage-gated K+ channels open

K+ leaves the axon → repolarisation back towards -70 mV.

K+ channels close slowly, so the membrane briefly overshoots to about -80 mV — hyperpolarisation.

The Na+/K+ pump then resets ion concentrations.

During and just after an AP, Na+ channels are inactivated — they can't reopen until the membrane resets.

This refractory period does three useful jobs:
1. Ensures AP travels in one direction only
2. Limits frequency of impulses
3. Allows discrete signals

All-or-nothing: size of stimulus changes frequency, not amplitude.
